subject: Biology
title: Chemical Coordination and Integration
summary: How the body coordinates itself with chemicals rather than nerves: what a hormone is, every endocrine gland of the human body from the hypothalamus to the ovary with its hormones, targets and disorders, the hormones made by the heart, kidney and gut, and the two mechanisms by which a hormone changes what a cell does. It is the last chapter of Human Physiology, the most memory-heavy chapter of Class 11, and the source of two to four NEET questions every year.

exam_profile.weightage: Class 11 Biology is a 70-mark theory paper set by the school on the CBSE pattern. Chemical Coordination and Integration is the closing chapter of Unit V, Human Physiology, which carries about 18 marks shared among Breathing and Exchange of Gases, Body Fluids and Circulation, Excretory Products, Locomotion and Movement, Neural Control and this chapter. In a typical school final this chapter alone gives 5 to 8 marks: two or three 1-mark items (an MCQ on which gland makes which hormone, which hormone is hyperglycemic or hypercalcemic, the second messenger of protein hormones, or the gland absent in one sex; and an Assertion-Reason on the posterior pituitary storing but not making oxytocin, or on adrenaline as the emergency hormone), a 2-mark or 3-mark question on a gland and its disorders, on insulin versus glucagon, or on PTH versus calcitonin, and every second year a 5-mark question on the hypothalamus-pituitary relationship, the adrenal gland with its layers, or the mechanism of hormone action with a diagram. NEET reliably takes two to four questions from this chapter, nearly all from NCERT tables and one-liners.

question_types.note: Gland-hormone matching (pineal-melatonin, thymus-thymosin, corpus luteum-progesterone, Leydig cells-androgens, juxtaglomerular cells-erythropoietin, atrial wall-ANF); hormone-effect matching (glucagon hyperglycemic, insulin hypoglycemic, PTH hypercalcemic, ANF lowers blood pressure, aldosterone retains Na<sup>+</sup>); the hormone not from the anterior pituitary (oxytocin, vasopressin); the second messenger (cyclic AMP, IP<sub>3</sub>, Ca<sup>2+</sup>); which receptor is on the membrane and which is intracellular; the organ without cortex and medulla (liver); the disorder not due to thyroid deficiency (exophthalmic goitre); the chemical nature of a hormone (oxytocin peptide, epinephrine amino-acid derivative, cortisol steroid, thyroxine iodothyronine); zona glomerulosa as the outermost layer; the number of parathyroid glands (four); the islets as 1 to 2 per cent of the pancreas.

Posterior pituitary is not a true endocrine gland because oxytocin and vasopressin are synthesised in the hypothalamus and only stored there; adrenaline is called the emergency hormone because it prepares the body for fight or flight; hypothalamic hormones reach the anterior pituitary by the portal circulation and not by general blood; goitre results from iodine deficiency because iodine is needed to synthesise thyroxine; steroid hormones have intracellular receptors because they are lipid-soluble and cross the membrane; insulin and glucagon are antagonistic; PTH and calcitonin are antagonistic; thymus degenerates in old age so immunity weakens; diabetes insipidus is due to ADH deficiency and not insulin deficiency.

Define hormone, endocrine gland, exocrine gland; why is the pancreas a composite (heterocrine) gland; why is the hypothalamus called the supreme commander or super master gland; name the hormones of the neurohypophysis and where they are made; name the two catecholamines; name the three layers of the adrenal cortex from outside in; what is a second messenger; name the hormones of the GI tract with one function each; name the hormone that lowers blood pressure and the one that raises blood calcium; distinguish diabetes mellitus from diabetes insipidus; what is cretinism and what causes it; name the gland absent in males and the one absent in females.

Hormones of the pars distalis with one function each; functions of thyroid hormones and effects of iodine deficiency; the role of PTH and calcitonin in calcium homeostasis; insulin versus glucagon in blood glucose regulation; functions of glucocorticoids and mineralocorticoids; the effects of adrenaline in an emergency; functions of testosterone or estrogen and progesterone; hormones of the heart, kidney and GI tract; the mechanism of action of FSH; the four chemical classes of hormones with an example each; differences between hypothyroidism and hyperthyroidism; why the elderly have weak immunity; a pregnant woman with a swollen neck (goitre, iodine, cretinism in the child).

The hypothalamus-pituitary axis with a labelled diagram: neurosecretory cells, portal circulation, adenohypophysis and neurohypophysis, releasing and inhibiting hormones, the six hormones of the pars distalis and the two of the pars nervosa; the adrenal gland with a labelled section and the hormones of the medulla and each cortical layer; the mechanism of hormone action comparing protein and steroid hormones with the two NCERT flow diagrams; the pancreas and diabetes mellitus (islets, insulin, glucagon, hyperglycemia, glycosuria, ketone bodies, insulin therapy); a labelled diagram of the location of endocrine glands with one hormone each; the thyroid gland: structure, hormones, functions and every disorder.

A passage on a patient passing large volumes of dilute urine (diabetes insipidus versus diabetes mellitus, ADH, the distal tubule), a passage on a woman from a hilly iodine-deficient region with a neck swelling and a pregnancy (goitre, thyroxine, BMR, cretinism), a passage on a student before an interview with sweating and a racing heart (adrenal medulla, catecholamines, fight or flight), a passage on a milk-ejection or jet-lag situation (neuroendocrine reflex, oxytocin; melatonin and the sleep-wake rhythm), or a passage on two women with different LH and estrogen readings (feedback loop defect versus ovary defect, straight from the exemplar).

sections.heading: Introduction: why chemical coordination is needed
sections.body:
You have just studied, in the previous chapter, how the nervous system coordinates the body. Nerves are fast and precise, but they have two limits that NCERT states plainly in the opening lines of this chapter. First, the neural system does not reach every cell of the body: nerve fibres innervate muscles, glands and organs, but a hepatocyte deep inside the liver or a bone cell inside its matrix has no nerve ending sitting on it. Second, cellular functions need to be regulated continuously, for hours and days, and a nerve impulse is a momentary event. So the body has a second, slower, chemical system that works through the blood. The endocrine system provides this chemical coordination, and the two systems together, neural and endocrine, coordinate and integrate the physiological functions of the body. That sentence is the answer to the 1-mark question 'why do we need chemical coordination in addition to neural coordination'.

The chapter is organised in four parts and you should keep the map in your head while revising. Part one defines endocrine glands and hormones. Part two, the bulk of the chapter, walks through the human endocrine system gland by gland: hypothalamus, pituitary, pineal, thyroid, parathyroid, thymus, adrenal, pancreas, testis and ovary. Part three lists hormones made by organs that are not primarily endocrine, the heart, kidney and gastrointestinal tract. Part four explains the mechanism of hormone action, the only part of the chapter that asks you to understand a process rather than remember a list. Examiners take 1-mark and 2-mark questions from parts one to three, and the diagram-based 5-mark questions from the pituitary, the adrenal and part four.
sections.tip: Learn the chapter as a table of gland, location, hormone, chemical nature, target, effect and disorder. Nearly every objective question is a cell of that table.

sections.heading: 19.1 Endocrine Glands and Hormones
sections.body:
Glands are of two kinds. An exocrine gland has a duct and pours its secretion through it onto a surface or into a cavity: salivary glands, sweat glands, the gastric glands and the exocrine part of the pancreas are examples. An endocrine gland lacks ducts, which is why NCERT calls endocrine glands ductless glands; its secretions, the hormones, are released directly into the blood and carried to distant target organs. The classical definition of a hormone was 'a chemical produced by an endocrine gland and released into the blood'. The current NCERT definition is broader and you should reproduce it word for word: hormones are non-nutrient chemicals which act as intercellular messengers and are produced in trace amounts. The three phrases are the three marking points. 'Non-nutrient' separates hormones from glucose and amino acids that also travel in blood. 'Intercellular messengers' says they carry information from one cell to another. 'Trace amounts' says they work at very low concentration, which is why a small deficiency or excess produces a disease.

Why did the definition change? Because it is now known that many organs that are not endocrine glands also make hormones. The gastrointestinal tract, the liver, the kidney and the heart all produce hormones (gastrin, erythropoietin, atrial natriuretic factor), and so do non-endocrine tissues in the form of growth factors. The new definition covers all of these. Together, the endocrine glands and the hormone-producing diffused tissues and cells located in different parts of the body constitute the endocrine system.

The organised endocrine glands of the human body, in the order NCERT lists them, are the pituitary, pineal, thyroid, parathyroid, adrenal, pancreas and the gonads (testis in males, ovary in females). The hypothalamus, though it is a part of the brain, is included because it makes hormones; and the thymus is included with the glands. Learn the locations from NCERT Fig. 19.1, because the exercise asks you to indicate them on a diagram: the pineal at the top of the brain stem on the dorsal side of the forebrain, the hypothalamus and pituitary at the base of the brain, the thyroid and parathyroids in the neck, the thymus behind the sternum, the adrenals on top of each kidney, the pancreas below the stomach, and the gonads in the scrotum or the pelvis.
sections.tip: Two-mark question: define exocrine gland, endocrine gland and hormone. Give the ductless / ducted contrast and the three-phrase NCERT definition of a hormone; each phrase is a mark.

sections.heading: 19.2.1 The Hypothalamus
sections.body:
The hypothalamus is the basal part of the diencephalon, the forebrain. Apart from regulating body temperature, hunger, thirst and other functions studied in the neural chapter, it is the master of the endocrine system, because it controls the pituitary, which in turn controls most of the other glands. That is why the pituitary is called the master gland and the hypothalamus the super master gland or supreme commander.

The hypothalamus contains several groups of neurosecretory cells called nuclei. These are neurons that behave like gland cells: they produce hormones. The hormones are of two kinds. Releasing hormones stimulate the secretion of pituitary hormones, and inhibiting hormones inhibit it. NCERT gives one example of each and both are asked. The gonadotrophin releasing hormone (GnRH) stimulates the pituitary to synthesise and release gonadotrophins (LH and FSH). Somatostatin inhibits the release of growth hormone from the pituitary. Other hypothalamic hormones you meet in the exemplar are thyrotrophin releasing hormone (TRH), corticotrophin releasing hormone (CRH), growth hormone releasing hormone (GHRH), prolactin releasing and inhibiting hormones and MSH releasing and inhibiting hormones. You do not need all of them for the school exam, but GnRH and somatostatin must be known with their effects.

How do these hormones reach the pituitary? The hypothalamic hormones originate in the neurons of the hypothalamus, travel down the axons and are released from the nerve endings, from where they reach the pituitary gland through a portal circulatory system. A portal system is one in which blood collected from one capillary bed is carried by a vein to a second capillary bed instead of returning to the heart. The hypophysial portal vessels collect the releasing and inhibiting hormones from the capillaries in the hypothalamus and deliver them straight to the capillaries of the anterior pituitary, so the hormones reach their target in high concentration without being diluted in the whole blood volume. This is the route for the anterior pituitary only. The posterior pituitary is regulated by the hypothalamus directly through neural connections: the axons of hypothalamic neurons run down into the posterior pituitary and release oxytocin and vasopressin there. So the hypothalamus controls the two lobes of the pituitary by two different routes, portal blood for the anterior lobe and axons for the posterior lobe, and this two-route contrast is a favourite 3-mark question.
sections.tip: Write 'portal circulation' for the anterior pituitary and 'neural (axonal) connection' for the posterior pituitary. Students who say the hypothalamic hormones travel through 'the blood' lose the mark; the examiner wants the word portal.

sections.heading: 19.2.2 The Pituitary Gland
sections.body:
The pituitary gland is located in a bony cavity called the sella turcica and is attached to the hypothalamus by a stalk. It is divided anatomically into an adenohypophysis and a neurohypophysis. The adenohypophysis has two portions, the pars distalis and the pars intermedia. The pars distalis, commonly called the anterior pituitary, produces six hormones: growth hormone (GH), prolactin (PRL), thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH), adrenocorticotrophic hormone (ACTH), luteinising hormone (LH) and follicle stimulating hormone (FSH). The pars intermedia secretes only one hormone, melanocyte stimulating hormone (MSH); in humans the pars intermedia is almost merged with the pars distalis. The neurohypophysis, or pars nervosa, is the posterior pituitary. It stores and releases two hormones, oxytocin and vasopressin, which are actually synthesised by the hypothalamus and are transported axonally to the neurohypophysis. This is the single most examined fact in the chapter: the posterior pituitary releases two hormones but makes neither.

Now the functions, in NCERT order, with the disorder attached to each where there is one. Growth hormone regulates the growth of the body. Its over-secretion stimulates abnormal growth of the body, leading to gigantism; low secretion results in stunted growth, pituitary dwarfism. Excess secretion of GH in adults, especially in middle age, cannot lengthen bones whose growth plates have closed, so it produces severe disfigurement, especially of the face, called acromegaly, which may lead to serious complications and even death if unchecked. Prolactin regulates the growth of the mammary glands and the formation of milk in them. TSH stimulates the synthesis and secretion of thyroid hormones from the thyroid gland. ACTH stimulates the synthesis and secretion of steroid hormones called glucocorticoids from the adrenal cortex. LH and FSH stimulate gonadal activity and are therefore called gonadotrophins. In males, LH stimulates the synthesis and secretion of androgens from the testis, and FSH together with the androgens regulates spermatogenesis. In females, LH induces ovulation of the fully mature follicle (the Graafian follicle) and maintains the corpus luteum formed from the remnants of the follicle after ovulation; FSH stimulates the growth and development of the ovarian follicles. MSH acts on the melanocytes and regulates the pigmentation of the skin.

Oxytocin acts on smooth muscles and stimulates their contraction. In females it stimulates a vigorous contraction of the uterus at the time of child birth and milk ejection from the mammary gland. Vasopressin acts mainly on the kidney and stimulates the reabsorption of water and electrolytes by the distal tubules, thereby reducing the loss of water through urine (diuresis); hence it is also called the anti-diuretic hormone (ADH). Its deficiency reduces water reabsorption, so a large volume of dilute urine is produced (diuresis) and the patient is always thirsty: this is diabetes insipidus. Note that it has nothing to do with insulin or glucose, and the urine contains no sugar, which is the distinction from diabetes mellitus that the examiner tests.
sections.tip: Exercise question 4 is a fill-in-the-blanks on targets: hypothalamic hormones act on the pituitary, TSH on the thyroid, ACTH on the adrenal cortex, gonadotrophins on the gonads (testis / ovary), MSH on the melanocytes of the skin. Learn this as a set.

sections.heading: 19.2.3 The Pineal Gland
sections.body:
The pineal gland is located on the dorsal side of the forebrain. It secretes a hormone called melatonin. Melatonin plays a very important role in the regulation of the 24-hour (diurnal) rhythm of our body. NCERT gives two examples of that rhythm and you should quote both: it helps in maintaining the normal rhythms of the sleep-wake cycle and of body temperature. In addition, melatonin also influences metabolism, pigmentation, the menstrual cycle and our defence capability. That is the whole NCERT paragraph, and it is enough for the 2-mark question 'name the hormone of the pineal gland and state two of its functions'.

The pineal appears in two exemplar questions that schools like to copy. The first asks which hormone regulates the sleep-wake cycle; the answer is melatonin, and the three distractors offered are usually thyroxine, insulin and adrenaline. The second is the jet-lag question. When you fly across several time zones, the light-dark cycle of the new place is out of step with the body's internal clock. Melatonin secretion, which rises in darkness and falls in light, is still timed to the old place, so you feel sleepy in the day and awake at night. The body clock (the suprachiasmatic nucleus of the hypothalamus, which controls the pineal) adjusts slowly over a few days, and the temporary sleep disturbance during this adjustment is jet lag. The exam answer is: jet lag is a temporary disturbance of the sleep-wake rhythm caused by rapid travel across time zones, because the melatonin rhythm set by the pineal gland is out of phase with the local light-dark cycle until it re-adjusts.

One more fact worth a mark: the pineal is the only endocrine gland whose secretion is directly governed by light, through the eyes and the hypothalamus, which is why it is sometimes called the biological clock of the body.
sections.tip: Do not write 'melanin' for the pineal hormone. Melanin is the skin pigment; melatonin is the pineal hormone; MSH is the pituitary hormone that stimulates melanocytes. Examiners see the three confused every year.

sections.heading: 19.2.4 Thyroid Gland
sections.body:
The thyroid gland is composed of two lobes located on either side of the trachea, interconnected by a thin flap of connective tissue called the isthmus. It is the largest endocrine gland. Under the microscope it is composed of follicles and stromal tissues. Each thyroid follicle is composed of follicular cells enclosing a cavity, and these follicular cells synthesise two hormones, tetraiodothyronine or thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3). The numbers tell you the iodine content: four atoms in T4, three in T3. Iodine is essential for the normal rate of hormone synthesis in the thyroid. Deficiency of iodine in the diet results in hypothyroidism and enlargement of the thyroid gland, commonly called goitre. The gland enlarges because low thyroxine removes the negative feedback on the pituitary, TSH rises, and the over-stimulated follicles multiply and swell even though they cannot make enough hormone.

The disorders form a compact list that every paper draws on. Hypothyroidism during pregnancy causes defective development and maturation of the growing baby, leading to stunted growth (cretinism), mental retardation, low intelligence quotient, abnormal skin and deaf-mutism. In adult women hypothyroidism may cause an irregular menstrual cycle; in adults generally it produces myxoedema, with low BMR, weight gain, lethargy and puffy skin. Due to cancer of the thyroid gland or the development of nodules of the thyroid, the rate of synthesis and secretion of thyroid hormones is increased to abnormal levels, leading to hyperthyroidism, which adversely affects the body physiology. Exophthalmic goitre is a form of hyperthyroidism characterised by enlargement of the thyroid gland, protrusion of the eyeballs, increased basal metabolic rate and weight loss; it is also called Graves' disease. Note the exemplar trap: exophthalmos is the one condition in the list that is not due to thyroid deficiency.

Functions of thyroid hormones, as NCERT lists them: they play an important role in the regulation of the basal metabolic rate; they support the process of red blood cell formation; they control the metabolism of carbohydrates, proteins and fats; and they help maintain water and electrolyte balance. The thyroid also secretes a protein hormone, thyrocalcitonin (TCT) or calcitonin, which regulates the blood calcium level by lowering it. Calcitonin is made by the parafollicular (C) cells between the follicles, not by the follicular cells, and it is a peptide, not an iodothyronine; both distinctions are used in MCQs.

Regulation is a simple negative feedback that examiners like as a flow chart: low T3/T4 in blood → hypothalamus releases TRH → anterior pituitary releases TSH → thyroid follicles synthesise and release T3/T4 → raised T3/T4 inhibits TRH and TSH release.
sections.tip: Cretinism is the childhood (or foetal) form of hypothyroidism; myxoedema the adult form; goitre is the swelling from iodine deficiency; Graves' disease is hyperthyroidism. A 2-mark question usually asks you to place two of these correctly.

sections.heading: 19.2.5 Parathyroid Gland
sections.body:
In humans, four parathyroid glands are present on the back side of the thyroid gland, one pair each in the two lobes of the thyroid gland. They secrete a peptide hormone called parathyroid hormone (PTH), also called parathormone. The secretion of PTH is regulated by the circulating levels of calcium ions: a fall in blood Ca2+ stimulates PTH release, a rise suppresses it. There is no pituitary trophic hormone controlling the parathyroid; it senses calcium directly, which is why it is called an independent gland in some questions.

PTH increases the Ca2+ level in the blood, and NCERT gives three routes, all three of which are needed for full marks. First, PTH acts on bones and stimulates the process of bone resorption (dissolution or demineralisation), releasing calcium from the skeleton into the blood. Second, PTH stimulates the reabsorption of Ca2+ by the renal tubules, so less is lost in urine. Third, it increases Ca2+ absorption from the digested food in the intestine (it does this through the activation of vitamin D, which the exemplar mentions). It is thus clear that PTH is a hypercalcemic hormone, that is, it increases the blood Ca2+ level. Along with TCT, it plays a significant role in calcium balance in the body.

The pairing with calcitonin is the classic 3-mark or 5-mark question on calcium homeostasis. When blood calcium is high, the thyroid releases calcitonin, which suppresses the release of calcium from bone and lowers blood calcium. When blood calcium is low, the parathyroids release PTH, which raises it by the three routes above. The two hormones are antagonistic and together they hold blood calcium within a narrow range. Why does the body care so much? Because calcium is needed for muscle contraction, nerve impulse transmission, blood clotting and as a second messenger. A fall in blood calcium causes the sustained muscle spasms of tetany that you met in the previous chapter; an excess weakens bones and produces kidney stones.

Hyposecretion of PTH (for instance after accidental removal of the parathyroids in thyroid surgery) causes hypocalcemia and tetany; hypersecretion causes demineralisation of bone and kidney stones. These clinical lines are not in NCERT but appear in school papers as a 1-mark extension.
sections.tip: Write all three targets of PTH: bone (resorption), kidney (reabsorption), intestine (absorption). The three verbs differ; the examiner looks for each.

sections.heading: 19.2.6 Thymus
sections.body:
The thymus gland is a lobular structure located on the dorsal side of the heart and the aorta, behind the sternum. It plays a major role in the development of the immune system. The thymus secretes peptide hormones called thymosins. Thymosins play a major role in the differentiation of T-lymphocytes, which provide cell-mediated immunity. In addition, thymosins also promote the production of antibodies to provide humoral immunity. Both halves of that sentence are marking points; a student who writes only 'T-cells' has given half the answer.

The point examiners like most is the age effect. The thymus is degenerated in old individuals, resulting in a decreased production of thymosins. As a result the immune responses of old persons become weak. This is the NCERT explanation for the exemplar question 'why do old people have a weak immune system', and it also appears as an Assertion-Reason item: Assertion, the immune response in old people is weak; Reason, the thymus degenerates with age and thymosin production falls; both true and R explains A.

Two facts tie this section to the rest of the syllabus. The thymus is a primary lymphoid organ (you will meet that phrase in Class 12, Human Health and Disease), where immature lymphocytes from the bone marrow mature into T-cells. And the exemplar contains a true-or-false statement that B-lymphocytes provide cell-mediated immunity: that statement is false, because B-cells produce antibodies for humoral immunity while T-cells are responsible for cell-mediated immunity. Also note from the exemplar MCQ on calcium: thymosin is the hormone not involved in calcium balance; vitamin D, PTH and thyrocalcitonin are.
sections.tip: Thymus makes thymosins (plural, peptides). Location: dorsal side of heart and aorta. Function: T-cell differentiation plus antibody production. Age: degenerates, so immunity falls. Four lines cover every question asked from this section.

sections.heading: 19.2.7 Adrenal Gland
sections.body:
Our body has one pair of adrenal glands, one at the anterior part of each kidney (the name means 'upon the kidney', hence suprarenal). The gland is composed of two types of tissues. The centrally located tissue is called the adrenal medulla, and outside this lies the adrenal cortex. The two parts have different origins, different hormones and different chemical classes of hormone, and a 5-mark question expects you to keep them apart.

Adrenal medulla. It secretes two hormones, adrenaline (epinephrine) and noradrenaline (norepinephrine), which are commonly called catecholamines; they are amino-acid derivatives. Adrenaline and noradrenaline are rapidly secreted in response to stress of any kind and during emergency situations, and are called emergency hormones or hormones of fight or flight. NCERT lists their effects and the list is a 3-mark question on its own: they increase alertness, dilate the pupils (pupillary dilation), cause piloerection (raising of hairs), sweating, an increase in heart beat and in the strength of heart contraction, and an increase in the rate of respiration. Catecholamines also stimulate the breakdown of glycogen (glycogenolysis), resulting in an increased concentration of glucose in the blood, and they stimulate the breakdown of lipids and proteins (lipolysis and proteolysis). The picture is of a body being readied for a burst of physical effort: more oxygen, more fuel, more blood flow.

Adrenal cortex. It can be divided into three layers, and NCERT names them from inside out, so be careful when a question asks for the outermost: the zona reticularis (inner layer), the zona fasciculata (middle layer) and the zona glomerulosa (outer layer). The cortex secretes many steroid hormones, commonly called corticoids. The corticoids involved in carbohydrate metabolism are glucocorticoids, and cortisol is the main one in our body. The corticoids that regulate the balance of water and electrolytes are mineralocorticoids, and aldosterone is the main one. Glucocorticoids stimulate gluconeogenesis, lipolysis and proteolysis, and inhibit the cellular uptake and utilisation of amino acids. Cortisol is also involved in maintaining cardio-vascular system and kidney functions, produces anti-inflammatory reactions, suppresses the immune response, and stimulates the production of RBCs. This is why cortisol-like drugs are used for allergies and after transplants. Aldosterone acts mainly on the renal tubules and stimulates the reabsorption of Na+ and water and the excretion of K+ and phosphate ions; it thus helps maintain electrolytes, body fluid volume, osmotic pressure and blood pressure. Small amounts of androgenic steroids are also secreted by the adrenal cortex, and these play a role in the growth of axial hair, pubic hair and facial hair during puberty.
sections.tip: Outermost layer of the cortex is the zona glomerulosa; NCERT's own list runs reticularis, fasciculata, glomerulosa from the inside. The exemplar VSA asks specifically for the outer layer.

sections.heading: 19.2.8 Pancreas
sections.body:
The pancreas is a composite gland (a heterocrine gland), which acts as both an exocrine and an endocrine gland. The exocrine part, the acini, pours pancreatic juice into the duodenum through a duct, as you studied in digestion. The endocrine pancreas consists of the islets of Langerhans. About 1 to 2 million islets are present in a normal human pancreas, yet they represent only 1 to 2 per cent of the pancreatic tissue. The two main types of cells in the islets are the α-cells, which secrete glucagon, and the β-cells, which secrete insulin. Both hormones are peptides.

Glucagon plays an important role in maintaining the normal blood glucose level. It acts mainly on liver cells (hepatocytes) and stimulates glycogenolysis, the breakdown of glycogen, resulting in an increased blood sugar (hyperglycemia). In addition, it stimulates gluconeogenesis, the synthesis of glucose from non-carbohydrate sources, which also contributes to hyperglycemia. Glucagon reduces the cellular glucose uptake and utilisation. Thus glucagon is a hyperglycemic hormone.

Insulin is a peptide hormone that also regulates glucose homeostasis. It acts mainly on hepatocytes and adipocytes (cells of adipose tissue) and enhances the cellular glucose uptake and utilisation. As a result there is a rapid movement of glucose from blood to the hepatocytes and adipocytes, causing a decrease in blood glucose (hypoglycemia). Insulin also stimulates the conversion of glucose to glycogen (glycogenesis) in the target cells. Insulin is therefore a hypoglycemic hormone. The glucose homeostasis of blood is thus maintained by the joint, antagonistic action of insulin and glucagon: when blood glucose rises after a meal, β-cells release insulin and glucose is stored; when it falls between meals, α-cells release glucagon and the stores are broken down.

Prolonged hyperglycemia leads to a complex disorder called diabetes mellitus, which is associated with the loss of glucose through urine and the formation of harmful compounds known as ketone bodies. Glucose spills into urine because it exceeds the reabsorption capacity of the renal tubules (the renal threshold); ketone bodies form because cells starved of glucose burn fats instead. Diabetic patients are successfully treated with insulin therapy. The exemplar adds a nuance worth knowing: diabetes can result either from an insulin deficiency or from insulin resistance, in which the cells fail to respond to insulin that is present.
sections.tip: Glucagon: glycogenolysis + gluconeogenesis, hyperglycemic, α-cells. Insulin: glucose uptake + glycogenesis, hypoglycemic, β-cells. Keep the three 'glyco' words apart; writing glycogenolysis for insulin is a common mark-losing slip.

sections.heading: 19.2.9 Testis
sections.body:
A pair of testes is present in the scrotal sac outside the abdomen of male individuals; the scrotum keeps them 2 to 2.5 °C below body temperature, which spermatogenesis needs. The testis performs a dual function: it is a primary sex organ that makes sperms and it is an endocrine gland. It is composed of seminiferous tubules and stromal or interstitial tissue. The Leydig cells or interstitial cells, which are present in the intertubular spaces, produce a group of hormones called androgens, mainly testosterone. Androgens are steroids.

NCERT gives the functions of androgens in one long sentence that you should split into points for a 3-mark answer. Androgens regulate the development, maturation and functions of the male accessory sex organs: the epididymis, vas deferens, seminal vesicles, prostate gland and urethra. They stimulate muscular growth, the growth of facial and axillary hair, aggressiveness and a low pitch of voice, that is, the male secondary sexual characters. They play a major stimulatory role in the process of spermatogenesis. They act on the central neural system and influence male sexual behaviour (libido). And they produce anabolic (synthetic) effects on protein and carbohydrate metabolism, which is the reason they are misused as performance-enhancing drugs, a point Class 12 returns to.

Control of the testis is by the pituitary gonadotrophins, and the exemplar asks the roles of LH in both sexes. In males, LH acts on the Leydig cells and stimulates the synthesis and secretion of androgens; FSH acts on the seminiferous tubules and, together with androgens, regulates spermatogenesis. The hypothalamus starts the chain with GnRH, and testosterone in turn inhibits GnRH and LH by negative feedback. The exercise question on the mechanism of action of FSH fits here: FSH is a protein (glycoprotein) hormone, so it binds to membrane receptors on its target cells, the Sertoli cells of the seminiferous tubules in males and the follicle cells of the ovary in females, generates a second messenger (cyclic AMP) inside the cell, and the second messenger activates the enzymes that carry out the cell's response, spermatogenesis in the testis and growth of the follicle in the ovary.
sections.tip: Leydig cells make testosterone; Sertoli cells (inside the tubules, from Class 12) nourish sperms. Only the Leydig-testosterone link is in this chapter, and it is what the MCQ 'Leydig cells produce' tests.

sections.heading: 19.2.10 Ovary
sections.body:
Females have a pair of ovaries located in the abdomen (the pelvic cavity). The ovary is the primary female sex organ, which produces one ovum during each menstrual cycle, and it is an endocrine gland. The ovary is composed of ovarian follicles and stromal tissues. It produces two groups of steroid hormones, estrogen and progesterone, and the timing of their secretion is what the examiner wants. Estrogen is synthesised and secreted mainly by the growing ovarian follicles. After ovulation, the ruptured follicle is converted to a structure called the corpus luteum, which secretes mainly progesterone. So follicle means estrogen and corpus luteum means progesterone; the exemplar MCQ 'the corpus luteum secretes' has progesterone as its answer.

Estrogens produce wide-ranging actions such as the stimulation of growth and activities of the female secondary sex organs (uterus, fallopian tubes, vagina), the development of growing ovarian follicles, the appearance of female secondary sex characters (for example a high pitch of voice, breast development, the pattern of fat and hair), and the development of mammary glands. Estrogens also regulate female sexual behaviour. Progesterone supports pregnancy: it prepares and maintains the uterine endometrium for the implanted embryo and suppresses uterine contractions. Progesterone also acts on the mammary glands and stimulates the formation of alveoli (sac-like structures which store milk) and milk secretion. NCERT calls it the progestational hormone in exercise 6, and that is the term the answer wants.

Control is again by the gonadotrophins, and the exemplar's feedback question is the cleverest thing set from this section. FSH stimulates the growth and development of ovarian follicles; the growing follicles secrete estrogen; LH induces ovulation of the fully mature Graafian follicle and maintains the corpus luteum. Rising estrogen normally feeds back to reduce LH secretion. Now the two clinical cases: an old woman whose blood shows high LH but low estrogen has ovaries (the gland X) that no longer respond to LH, as happens after menopause when the follicles are exhausted, so the pituitary keeps pushing without result. A woman with high LH and high estrogen has a defect in the negative feedback loop, because her high estrogen is failing to switch LH off.
sections.tip: Exercise 6 asks for the progestational hormone (progesterone), the gonadotrophic hormones (LH and FSH), and 'androgens and estrogens' (testosterone; estradiol). Have the one-word answers ready.

sections.heading: 19.3 Hormones of Heart, Kidney and Gastrointestinal Tract
sections.body:
As mentioned earlier, hormones are also secreted by some tissues which are not endocrine glands. This short section produces a surprising number of 1-mark questions, because each organ has one hormone with one crisp function.

Heart. The atrial wall of our heart secretes a very important peptide hormone called atrial natriuretic factor (ANF), which decreases blood pressure. When blood pressure is increased, ANF is secreted, which causes dilation of the blood vessels; this reduces the blood pressure. 'Natriuretic' means it also promotes the excretion of sodium in urine, which lowers blood volume. ANF is the 'blood pressure lowering hormone' of exercise 6(e) and it works in the opposite direction to aldosterone and vasopressin.

Kidney. The juxtaglomerular cells of the kidney produce a peptide hormone called erythropoietin, which stimulates erythropoiesis, the formation of RBCs, in the bone marrow. It is released when the oxygen supply to the kidney falls, which is why people living at high altitude have more red cells and why kidney failure causes anaemia. Keep erythropoietin distinct from renin, an enzyme from the same cells that you met in the excretion chapter.

Gastrointestinal tract. Endocrine cells present in different parts of the GI tract secrete four major peptide hormones. Gastrin acts on the gastric glands and stimulates the secretion of hydrochloric acid and pepsinogen. Secretin acts on the exocrine pancreas and stimulates the secretion of water and bicarbonate ions, which neutralise the acid chyme entering the duodenum. Cholecystokinin (CCK) acts on both the pancreas and the gall bladder and stimulates the secretion of pancreatic enzymes and bile juice respectively. Gastric inhibitory peptide (GIP) inhibits gastric secretion and motility. Read the names as instructions: gastr-in stimulates the gastric glands, secret-in makes the pancreas secrete, chole-cysto-kinin moves the bile bladder, and gastric inhibitory peptide inhibits the stomach.

Finally NCERT notes that several non-endocrine tissues secrete hormones called growth factors, which are essential for the normal growth of tissues and their repair or regeneration. This is the reason the definition of a hormone was widened in section 19.1.
sections.tip: Exercise 3 asks the hormones of atrium, kidney and GI tract: ANF; erythropoietin; gastrin, secretin, CCK, GIP. Write the full name of each abbreviation at least once in the answer.

sections.heading: 19.4 Mechanism of Hormone Action
sections.body:
Hormones produce their effects on target tissues by binding to specific proteins called hormone receptors located in the target tissues only. Receptors are of two kinds. Membrane-bound receptors are present on the cell membrane of the target cells. Intracellular receptors are present inside the target cell, mostly in the nucleus, and are therefore also called nuclear receptors. The binding of a hormone to its receptor leads to the formation of a hormone-receptor complex. Each receptor is specific to one hormone only, and hence receptors are said to be specific. That specificity is the reason a hormone circulating in the whole blood acts only on its target cells: only they carry the receptor. The formation of the hormone-receptor complex leads to certain biochemical changes in the target tissue, and target tissue metabolism and hence physiological functions are regulated by hormones.

On the basis of their chemical nature, hormones can be divided into four groups, and this classification decides which kind of receptor a hormone uses. (i) Peptide, polypeptide and protein hormones: insulin, glucagon, the pituitary hormones, the hypothalamic hormones (and also PTH, calcitonin, thymosins, ANF, erythropoietin and the gut hormones). (ii) Steroids: cortisol, aldosterone, testosterone, estradiol and progesterone. (iii) Iodothyronines: the thyroid hormones T3 and T4. (iv) Amino-acid derivatives: epinephrine and norepinephrine (and melatonin).

Protein and peptide hormones are water-soluble and cannot cross the lipid bilayer, so they act through membrane-bound receptors. The hormone (the first messenger) binds to the receptor on the outer surface; the complex activates an enzyme inside the membrane (adenylate cyclase for the cAMP pathway), which generates a second messenger inside the cell. NCERT names three second messengers: cyclic AMP, IP3 (inositol trisphosphate) and Ca2+. The second messenger activates a cascade of enzymes (protein kinases), which in turn regulate cellular metabolism, so the hormone's message is amplified and delivered without the hormone ever entering the cell. This is NCERT Fig. 19.5(a) and it must be drawn as: hormone → membrane receptor → second messenger (cAMP) → biochemical responses (enzyme activation) → physiological response.

Steroid hormones and iodothyronines are lipid-soluble and pass through the plasma membrane. Inside the cell they bind to intracellular receptors, and the hormone-receptor complex enters the nucleus and interacts with the genome (DNA). This interaction regulates gene expression or chromosome function, switching particular genes on or off. Cumulative biochemical actions, the synthesis of new proteins directed by the switched-on genes, result in physiological and developmental effects. This is Fig. 19.5(b): hormone → intracellular receptor → hormone-receptor complex → genome interaction → gene expression (protein synthesis) → physiological and developmental effects. The two mechanisms differ in speed too: second-messenger responses are fast (adrenaline acts within seconds), gene-expression responses are slow but long lasting (thyroxine and testosterone act over days).
sections.tip: The 5-mark question is 'compare the mechanism of action of a protein hormone and a steroid hormone with diagrams'. Four contrasts earn it: solubility, receptor location, second messenger versus gene expression, speed. Then the two flow diagrams.

key_terms.definition: A non-nutrient chemical which acts as an intercellular messenger and is produced in trace amounts (NCERT). Released into blood and acting on distant target cells that carry its specific receptor.
A ductless gland whose secretions (hormones) are released directly into the blood, e.g. thyroid, pituitary. Contrast with an exocrine gland, which has a duct, e.g. salivary gland.
Neurons of the hypothalamic nuclei that synthesise and release hormones (releasing and inhibiting hormones, oxytocin and vasopressin) instead of neurotransmitters alone.

Hypothalamic hormones that respectively stimulate (e.g. GnRH) or inhibit (e.g. somatostatin) the secretion of hormones by the anterior pituitary; they reach it through the hypophysial portal circulation.

A vascular arrangement in which blood from the capillaries of the hypothalamus is carried by portal veins to a second capillary bed in the anterior pituitary, delivering hypothalamic hormones directly to their target.

The two parts of the pituitary. Adenohypophysis = pars distalis (six hormones) + pars intermedia (MSH); neurohypophysis or pars nervosa = posterior pituitary, which stores and releases oxytocin and vasopressin made in the hypothalamus.
LH and FSH of the anterior pituitary, which stimulate the activity of the gonads: LH induces ovulation and androgen secretion; FSH stimulates follicle growth and, with androgens, spermatogenesis.

Posterior pituitary hormone that stimulates reabsorption of water and electrolytes by the distal tubules of the kidney, reducing water loss in urine (diuresis). Its deficiency causes diabetes insipidus.
Enlargement of the thyroid gland, commonly due to iodine deficiency in the diet, which reduces thyroxine synthesis (hypothyroidism).
Stunted growth with mental retardation, low IQ, abnormal skin and deaf-mutism in a child, caused by hypothyroidism during pregnancy and infancy.
A form of hyperthyroidism with enlargement of the thyroid, protrusion of the eyeballs, increased BMR and weight loss.
A hormone that raises blood Ca<sup>2+</sup>: parathyroid hormone, acting by bone resorption, renal reabsorption and intestinal absorption of calcium. Calcitonin is its antagonist.

Peptide hormones of the thymus that promote differentiation of T-lymphocytes (cell-mediated immunity) and antibody production (humoral immunity); their fall with thymus degeneration weakens immunity in old age.
Adrenaline (epinephrine) and noradrenaline (norepinephrine), amino-acid-derivative hormones of the adrenal medulla; the emergency or fight-or-flight hormones.

Steroid corticoids of the adrenal cortex. Glucocorticoids (mainly cortisol) act on carbohydrate metabolism, are anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive; mineralocorticoids (mainly aldosterone) regulate Na<sup>+</sup>, K<sup>+</sup>, water balance and blood pressure.
The endocrine tissue of the pancreas: 1 to 2 million islets forming 1 to 2 per cent of the gland; α-cells secrete glucagon and β-cells secrete insulin.
Glucagon raises blood glucose by glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis; insulin lowers it by promoting glucose uptake and glycogenesis in hepatocytes and adipocytes.

Prolonged hyperglycemia due to insulin deficiency or resistance, with loss of glucose in urine and formation of ketone bodies; treated with insulin therapy. Distinct from diabetes insipidus (ADH deficiency, no glycosuria).
Cells in the intertubular spaces of the testis that secrete androgens, mainly testosterone, under the stimulation of LH.
The yellow body formed from the ruptured ovarian follicle after ovulation; it secretes mainly progesterone and is maintained by LH.
Peptide hormone of the atrial wall released when blood pressure rises; it dilates blood vessels and lowers blood pressure.
Peptide hormone of the juxtaglomerular cells of the kidney that stimulates erythropoiesis (RBC formation) in the bone marrow.
An intracellular molecule (cyclic AMP, IP<sub>3</sub> or Ca<sup>2+</sup>) generated when a protein hormone binds its membrane receptor; it activates enzyme cascades that produce the cell's response.

A receptor inside the target cell, mostly in the nucleus, used by lipid-soluble steroid hormones and iodothyronines; the hormone-receptor complex interacts with the genome and regulates gene expression.

formula_sheet.name: Definition of a hormone (NCERT)
formula_sheet.expr: Non-nutrient chemicals which act as intercellular messengers and are produced in trace amounts
formula_sheet.note: Endocrine glands are ductless; secretions go directly into blood. Exocrine glands have ducts.

formula_sheet.name: Hypothalamus
formula_sheet.expr: Neurosecretory cells (nuclei) → releasing hormones (GnRH stimulates LH/FSH release) and inhibiting hormones (somatostatin inhibits GH). Reach anterior pituitary by portal circulation; posterior pituitary by neural (axonal) connection
formula_sheet.note: Also synthesises oxytocin and vasopressin, which are stored in the neurohypophysis.

formula_sheet.name: Pituitary: parts and hormones
formula_sheet.expr: Sella turcica. Adenohypophysis = pars distalis (GH, PRL, TSH, ACTH, LH, FSH) + pars intermedia (MSH). Neurohypophysis / pars nervosa = oxytocin, vasopressin (ADH)
formula_sheet.note: Disorders: GH excess in childhood gigantism, GH deficiency dwarfism, GH excess in adults acromegaly; ADH deficiency diabetes insipidus.

formula_sheet.name: Targets of the pituitary trophic hormones
formula_sheet.expr: TSH → thyroid; ACTH → adrenal cortex (glucocorticoids); LH, FSH → gonads; PRL → mammary glands; MSH → melanocytes; GH → whole body; oxytocin → uterus, mammary gland; ADH → distal tubules of kidney

formula_sheet.name: Pineal gland
formula_sheet.expr: Dorsal side of forebrain; melatonin; 24-hour (diurnal) rhythm: sleep-wake cycle and body temperature; also metabolism, pigmentation, menstrual cycle, defence capability
formula_sheet.note: Jet lag = melatonin rhythm out of phase with the new light-dark cycle.

formula_sheet.name: Thyroid
formula_sheet.expr: Two lobes + isthmus; follicles (follicular cells) make T<sub>4</sub> (thyroxine) and T<sub>3</sub>; iodine essential. TCT (calcitonin, protein) lowers blood Ca<sup>2+</sup>. Functions: BMR, RBC formation, metabolism of carbohydrate/protein/fat, water and electrolyte balance
formula_sheet.note: Hypo: goitre (iodine deficiency), cretinism (child), myxoedema (adult), irregular menses. Hyper: nodules/cancer; exophthalmic goitre = Graves' disease.

formula_sheet.name: Parathyroid
formula_sheet.expr: Four glands on the back of the thyroid; PTH (peptide) regulated by blood Ca<sup>2+</sup>; raises Ca<sup>2+</sup> by bone resorption, renal tubular reabsorption and intestinal absorption
formula_sheet.note: Hypercalcemic hormone; antagonist of calcitonin; together maintain calcium balance.

formula_sheet.name: Thymus
formula_sheet.expr: Lobular; dorsal side of heart and aorta; thymosins (peptide) → differentiation of T-lymphocytes (cell-mediated immunity) + antibody production (humoral immunity)
formula_sheet.note: Degenerates in old age → low thymosin → weak immunity.

formula_sheet.name: Adrenal gland
formula_sheet.expr: Medulla: adrenaline + noradrenaline (catecholamines, emergency / fight-or-flight): alertness, pupil dilation, piloerection, sweating, heart rate and force, respiration, glycogenolysis, lipolysis, proteolysis. Cortex (outer → inner): zona glomerulosa, zona fasciculata, zona reticularis; corticoids = glucocorticoids (cortisol: gluconeogenesis, anti-inflammatory, immunosuppressive, RBC production) + mineralocorticoids (aldosterone: Na<sup>+</sup> and water reabsorption, K<sup>+</sup> and phosphate excretion) + small androgens (axial, pubic, facial hair)
formula_sheet.note: Located at the anterior (superior) part of each kidney.

formula_sheet.name: Pancreas
formula_sheet.expr: Composite gland; islets of Langerhans 1 to 2 million, 1 to 2 per cent of tissue; α-cells glucagon (glycogenolysis + gluconeogenesis, hyperglycemic); β-cells insulin (glucose uptake by hepatocytes and adipocytes + glycogenesis, hypoglycemic)
formula_sheet.note: Diabetes mellitus: prolonged hyperglycemia, glucose in urine, ketone bodies; insulin therapy.

formula_sheet.name: Gonads
formula_sheet.expr: Testis: Leydig (interstitial) cells → androgens (testosterone): accessory sex organs, secondary sexual characters, spermatogenesis, anabolic. Ovary: growing follicles → estrogen (secondary sex organs and characters, follicle development, mammary glands); corpus luteum → progesterone (pregnancy, alveoli and milk secretion)
formula_sheet.note: LH: androgen secretion in males; ovulation + corpus luteum in females. FSH: spermatogenesis with androgens; follicle growth.

formula_sheet.name: Hormones of non-endocrine organs
formula_sheet.expr: Atrial wall → ANF (lowers BP by vasodilation). Kidney juxtaglomerular cells → erythropoietin (erythropoiesis). GI tract → gastrin (HCl + pepsinogen), secretin (water + HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> from pancreas), CCK (pancreatic enzymes + bile), GIP (inhibits gastric secretion and motility)
formula_sheet.note: All peptides. Non-endocrine tissues also make growth factors.

formula_sheet.name: Chemical classes of hormones
formula_sheet.expr: (i) Peptide/protein: insulin, glucagon, pituitary and hypothalamic hormones; (ii) steroids: cortisol, testosterone, estradiol, progesterone; (iii) iodothyronines: T<sub>3</sub>, T<sub>4</sub>; (iv) amino-acid derivatives: epinephrine
formula_sheet.note: Classes (i) and (iv) use membrane receptors; (ii) and (iii) use intracellular receptors.

formula_sheet.name: Mechanism of hormone action
formula_sheet.expr: Protein hormone → membrane-bound receptor → second messenger (cyclic AMP, IP<sub>3</sub>, Ca<sup>2+</sup>) → enzyme activation → regulation of metabolism. Steroid / iodothyronine → enters cell → intracellular (nuclear) receptor → hormone-receptor complex → genome → gene expression → physiological and developmental effects
formula_sheet.note: Receptors are specific to one hormone; that is why hormones act only on target cells.

diagrams.title: Location of endocrine glands in the human body (NCERT Fig. 19.1)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw a simple outline of the human body, front view. In the head draw the brain and mark the pineal gland as a small dot on the dorsal upper part of the brain stem, and the hypothalamus with the pituitary hanging below it at the base of the brain. In the neck draw the butterfly-shaped thyroid across the trachea and mark the parathyroids as four dots on its back. Behind the sternum, above the heart, draw the lobular thymus. Below the diaphragm draw the two kidneys with an adrenal gland capping the top of each, and the pancreas lying horizontally below the stomach. In the pelvis draw the ovaries (female) or, below the trunk, the testes in the scrotum (male). Label all nine: pineal, hypothalamus, pituitary, thyroid, parathyroid, thymus, adrenal, pancreas, testis/ovary. Examiners award the mark per correct label and position; a female figure should show ovaries and a male one testes, never both.

diagrams.title: Hypothalamus-pituitary relationship (NCERT Fig. 19.2)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw the hypothalamus as a rounded region at the top with two or three neurosecretory cells drawn as neurons with cell bodies in the hypothalamus. Show a stalk leading down to the pituitary, drawn as two lobes side by side: the anterior pituitary (adenohypophysis, pars distalis) on the left and the posterior pituitary (neurohypophysis, pars nervosa) on the right. From the first group of neurosecretory cells draw short axons ending on a capillary network in the stalk (median eminence); from this capillary bed draw the portal vein running down into a second capillary network in the anterior pituitary, and label it hypophysial portal vessel. From the second group of neurosecretory cells draw long axons passing straight down through the stalk into the posterior pituitary, ending near capillaries; label them and write oxytocin and vasopressin. Label: hypothalamus, neurosecretory cells, portal circulation, anterior pituitary, posterior pituitary, releasing/inhibiting hormones entering the portal blood, and the six anterior hormones leaving. The diagram must make the two routes visible: blood to the anterior lobe, axons to the posterior lobe.

diagrams.title: Thyroid and parathyroid glands with the isthmus (NCERT Fig. 19.3)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw the trachea as a vertical tube with cartilage rings, with the larynx at the top. Draw the two lobes of the thyroid as elongated ovals on either side of the upper trachea, joined across the front by a narrow bridge below the larynx; label this bridge the isthmus. For the back view draw the two lobes again and place four small ovals, two on each lobe (one upper, one lower), and label them parathyroid glands. Label: larynx, trachea, thyroid lobes (right and left), isthmus, parathyroid glands. If asked, add a small inset circle of thyroid histology showing follicles as rings of follicular cells around a colloid-filled cavity, with stromal tissue between, and label follicle, follicular cell and colloid.

diagrams.title: Section of the adrenal gland (NCERT Fig. 19.4)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw a kidney and cap its upper pole with a triangular adrenal gland. Beside it draw an enlarged vertical section of the adrenal as a broad band: the outer thick cortex and the inner medulla. Divide the cortex into three layers with horizontal lines and label them from the outside in: zona glomerulosa (outer, cells in clusters), zona fasciculata (middle, widest, cells in columns), zona reticularis (inner, cells in a net). Label the medulla at the centre and show a capsule on the outside. Write the hormones beside each region: glomerulosa - mineralocorticoids (aldosterone); fasciculata - glucocorticoids (cortisol); reticularis - androgens; medulla - adrenaline and noradrenaline. Eight labels: capsule, cortex, medulla, the three zonae, kidney, adrenal gland.

diagrams.title: Mechanism of action of a protein hormone (NCERT Fig. 19.5a)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw a rectangle for the target cell with a thick boundary for the plasma membrane and an oval nucleus inside. Outside the membrane draw the hormone as a small shape approaching a receptor drawn as a matching notch embedded in the membrane; label hormone (first messenger) and membrane-bound receptor. Draw an arrow from the receptor into the cytoplasm to a labelled box 'second messenger (cyclic AMP, IP<sub>3</sub>, Ca<sup>2+</sup>)'. From the second messenger draw an arrow to 'biochemical responses (enzyme activation, cascade)' and then to 'physiological responses'. The hormone must stay outside the cell; drawing it inside is the error that loses the mark. Labels: hormone, receptor, plasma membrane, second messenger, enzyme activation, physiological response, nucleus.

diagrams.title: Mechanism of action of a steroid hormone (NCERT Fig. 19.5b)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw the same target cell. This time draw the hormone passing through the plasma membrane into the cytoplasm (arrow crossing the membrane) and binding to an intracellular receptor drawn as a shape in the cytoplasm or inside the nucleus; label the hormone-receptor complex. Draw the complex moving into the nucleus and touching a wavy line labelled DNA or genome. From there draw an arrow labelled gene expression to mRNA and then to protein synthesis in the cytoplasm, ending in a box 'physiological and developmental effects'. Labels: steroid hormone, plasma membrane, intracellular (nuclear) receptor, hormone-receptor complex, genome/DNA, gene expression, protein synthesis, physiological and developmental effects. Draw 19.5(a) and 19.5(b) side by side when asked to compare.

diagrams.title: Feedback regulation of the thyroid (TRH-TSH-thyroxine axis)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw three boxes vertically: hypothalamus at the top, anterior pituitary in the middle, thyroid gland at the bottom, and a fourth box to the side labelled target cells (BMR). Draw a downward arrow from hypothalamus to pituitary labelled TRH, from pituitary to thyroid labelled TSH, and from thyroid to target cells labelled T<sub>3</sub> and T<sub>4</sub>. Then draw two curved arrows from the thyroid hormone back up to the pituitary and to the hypothalamus with a minus sign, labelled negative feedback. Add a note that low iodine keeps T<sub>3</sub>/T<sub>4</sub> low, feedback fails, TSH rises and the gland enlarges into a goitre. The same skeleton, with CRH, ACTH and cortisol, gives the adrenal axis, and with GnRH, LH/FSH and sex steroids gives the gonadal axis.

diagrams.title: Regulation of blood glucose by insulin and glucagon
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw a horizontal line labelled normal blood glucose. Above it write 'blood glucose rises (after a meal)' with an arrow to a box 'β-cells of islets of Langerhans → insulin'. From insulin draw arrows to 'glucose uptake by hepatocytes and adipocytes' and 'glycogenesis (glucose → glycogen)', and a final arrow back down to the line labelled blood glucose falls. Below the line write 'blood glucose falls (between meals)' with an arrow to 'α-cells → glucagon', then arrows to 'glycogenolysis (glycogen → glucose) in liver' and 'gluconeogenesis', and an arrow back up labelled blood glucose rises. Mark insulin hypoglycemic and glucagon hyperglycemic, and add a side note: insulin deficiency → prolonged hyperglycemia → diabetes mellitus (glycosuria, ketone bodies). The same two-sided layout with PTH (raises Ca<sup>2+</sup>: bone resorption, renal reabsorption, intestinal absorption) and calcitonin (lowers Ca<sup>2+</sup>) gives the calcium homeostasis chart.

ncert_questions.q: Define the following: (a) Exocrine gland (b) Endocrine gland (c) Hormone
ncert_questions.a:
(a) Exocrine gland: A gland that has a duct and releases its secretion through the duct onto a surface or into a cavity, e.g. salivary glands, sweat glands, gastric glands, the exocrine part of the pancreas.

(b) Endocrine gland: A ductless gland whose secretions, the hormones, are released directly into the blood and carried to distant target organs, e.g. thyroid, pituitary, adrenal.

(c) Hormone: Non-nutrient chemicals which act as intercellular messengers and are produced in trace amounts. They are secreted into the blood and act on specific target cells that possess receptors for them, e.g. insulin, thyroxine.

ncert_questions.q: Diagrammatically indicate the location of the various endocrine glands in our body.
ncert_questions.a: Draw the outline of the human body and mark: pineal gland on the dorsal side of the forebrain; hypothalamus at the base of the brain (diencephalon) with the pituitary gland below it in the sella turcica; thyroid gland in the neck on either side of the trachea with the four parathyroid glands on its back; thymus behind the sternum on the dorsal side of the heart and aorta; one adrenal gland on the anterior (upper) part of each kidney; the pancreas below the stomach; testes in the scrotum (male) or ovaries in the pelvic cavity (female). Nine labels in all; use NCERT Fig. 19.1 as the model.

ncert_questions.q: List the hormones secreted by the following: (a) Hypothalamus (b) Pituitary (c) Thyroid (d) Parathyroid (e) Adrenal (f) Pancreas (g) Testis (h) Ovary (i) Thymus (j) Atrium (k) Kidney (l) G-I Tract
ncert_questions.a:
(a) Hypothalamus: releasing hormones (e.g. GnRH, TRH, CRH, GHRH) and inhibiting hormones (e.g. somatostatin); also synthesises oxytocin and vasopressin.

(b) Pituitary: pars distalis: GH, prolactin, TSH, ACTH, LH, FSH; pars intermedia: MSH; neurohypophysis releases oxytocin and vasopressin (ADH).

(c) Thyroid: thyroxine (T4), triiodothyronine (T3) and thyrocalcitonin (calcitonin).

(d) Parathyroid: parathyroid hormone (PTH, parathormone).

(e) Adrenal: medulla: adrenaline (epinephrine) and noradrenaline (norepinephrine); cortex: glucocorticoids (cortisol), mineralocorticoids (aldosterone) and small amounts of androgens.

(f) Pancreas: glucagon (α-cells) and insulin (β-cells).

(g) Testis: androgens, mainly testosterone.

(h) Ovary: estrogen (growing follicles) and progesterone (corpus luteum).

(i) Thymus: thymosins.

(j) Atrium: atrial natriuretic factor (ANF).

(k) Kidney: erythropoietin.

(l) G-I tract: gastrin, secretin, cholecystokinin (CCK), gastric inhibitory peptide (GIP).

ncert_questions.q: Fill in the blanks: Hormones — Target gland. (a) Hypothalamic hormones → ______ (b) Thyrotrophin (TSH) → ______ (c) Corticotrophin (ACTH) → ______ (d) Gonadotrophins (LH, FSH) → ______ (e) Melanotrophin (MSH) → ______
ncert_questions.a: (a) Hypothalamic hormones → pituitary gland (anterior pituitary). (b) TSH → thyroid gland. (c) ACTH → adrenal cortex. (d) LH, FSH → gonads (testis in males, ovary in females). (e) MSH → melanocytes of the skin.

ncert_questions.q: Write short notes on the functions of the following hormones: (a) Parathyroid hormone (PTH) (b) Thyroid hormones (c) Thymosins (d) Androgens (e) Estrogens (f) Insulin and Glucagon
ncert_questions.a:
(a) PTH: A peptide hormone of the four parathyroid glands, secreted when blood Ca2+ falls. It raises blood calcium by stimulating bone resorption (demineralisation), reabsorption of Ca2+ by the renal tubules and absorption of Ca2+ from digested food. It is a hypercalcemic hormone and, with calcitonin, maintains calcium balance.

(b) Thyroid hormones (T3, T4): Regulate the basal metabolic rate; support RBC formation; control the metabolism of carbohydrates, proteins and fats; maintain water and electrolyte balance; needed for normal growth and development of the brain in the foetus and infant. Calcitonin from the thyroid lowers blood calcium.

(c) Thymosins: Peptide hormones of the thymus that bring about differentiation of T-lymphocytes for cell-mediated immunity and promote antibody production for humoral immunity. Their decline with age weakens immunity.

(d) Androgens (testosterone): Regulate the development, maturation and functions of the male accessory sex organs (epididymis, vas deferens, seminal vesicles, prostate, urethra); produce male secondary sexual characters (muscular growth, facial and axillary hair, aggressiveness, low-pitched voice); stimulate spermatogenesis; influence male sexual behaviour; have anabolic effects on protein and carbohydrate metabolism.

(e) Estrogens: Stimulate growth and activity of the female secondary sex organs, the development of the ovarian follicles, the appearance of female secondary sexual characters (high-pitched voice, breast development) and the development of the mammary glands; regulate female sexual behaviour.

(f) Insulin and glucagon: Both from the islets of Langerhans. Insulin (β-cells) lowers blood glucose by increasing glucose uptake and utilisation by hepatocytes and adipocytes and by stimulating glycogenesis (hypoglycemic). Glucagon (α-cells) raises blood glucose by stimulating glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis in the liver and reducing cellular glucose uptake (hyperglycemic). Together they maintain glucose homeostasis.

ncert_questions.q: Give example(s) of: (a) Hyperglycemic hormone and hypoglycemic hormone (b) Hypercalcemic hormone (c) Gonadotrophic hormones (d) Progestational hormone (e) Blood pressure lowering hormone (f) Androgens and estrogens
ncert_questions.a: (a) Hyperglycemic hormone: glucagon (also adrenaline and cortisol); hypoglycemic hormone: insulin. (b) Hypercalcemic hormone: parathyroid hormone (PTH). (c) Gonadotrophic hormones: LH and FSH. (d) Progestational hormone: progesterone. (e) Blood pressure lowering hormone: atrial natriuretic factor (ANF). (f) Androgen: testosterone; estrogen: estradiol.

ncert_questions.q: Which hormonal deficiency is responsible for the following: (a) Diabetes mellitus (b) Goitre (c) Cretinism
ncert_questions.a: (a) Diabetes mellitus: deficiency of insulin (from the β-cells of the islets of Langerhans), or failure of cells to respond to it. (b) Goitre: deficiency of thyroxine (thyroid hormones) usually because of iodine deficiency in the diet; the low thyroxine raises TSH, which enlarges the gland. (c) Cretinism: deficiency of thyroid hormones (hypothyroidism) during pregnancy and infancy.

ncert_questions.q: Briefly mention the mechanism of action of FSH.
ncert_questions.a: FSH is a protein (glycoprotein) hormone, so it acts through a membrane-bound receptor. (i) FSH binds to its specific receptor on the plasma membrane of the target cells (Sertoli cells of the seminiferous tubules in the testis; follicular cells of the ovary). (ii) The hormone-receptor complex activates an enzyme in the membrane that generates a second messenger, cyclic AMP, inside the cell. (iii) The second messenger activates a cascade of enzymes that alter the metabolism of the cell. (iv) The result is the physiological response: in males, FSH with androgens stimulates spermatogenesis; in females it stimulates the growth and development of the ovarian follicles and their secretion of estrogen. FSH does not enter the cell and does not act on the genome directly.

ncert_questions.q: Match the following: Column I: (a) T<sub>4</sub> (b) PTH (c) GnRH (d) LH. Column II: (i) Hypothalamus (ii) Thyroid (iii) Pituitary (iv) Parathyroid
ncert_questions.a: (a) T4 → (ii) Thyroid. (b) PTH → (iv) Parathyroid. (c) GnRH → (i) Hypothalamus. (d) LH → (iii) Pituitary.

ncert_questions.q: A pregnant woman from a hilly region shows a swelling in the front of the neck. Name the disorder, give its cause, and state how it can affect her baby.
ncert_questions.a: Disorder: goitre, an enlargement of the thyroid gland. Cause: deficiency of iodine in the diet, common in hilly regions where the soil and water are poor in iodine. Iodine is essential for the synthesis of thyroxine; low thyroxine removes the feedback inhibition on the pituitary, TSH rises and over-stimulates the thyroid, which enlarges (hypothyroidism with goitre). Effect on the baby: hypothyroidism during pregnancy causes defective development and maturation of the growing foetus, leading to cretinism: stunted growth, mental retardation, low IQ, abnormal skin and deaf-mutism. Prevention is iodised salt.

ncert_questions.q: A milkman is very upset one morning as his cow refuses to give any milk. The milkman's wife gets the calf from the shed. On fondling by the calf, the cow gives sufficient milk. Describe the role of the endocrine gland and the pathway associated with this response.
ncert_questions.a: The response is a neuroendocrine reflex. Suckling or fondling of the udder by the calf stimulates sensory nerve endings in the teat; the impulses travel to the hypothalamus. The neurosecretory cells of the hypothalamus synthesise oxytocin, which is transported along their axons and stored in the posterior pituitary (neurohypophysis). The nerve impulses trigger the release of oxytocin from the posterior pituitary into the blood. Oxytocin reaches the mammary gland and causes contraction of the smooth (myoepithelial) cells around the alveoli and ducts, which ejects the stored milk. Pathway: udder stimulus by calf → sensory nerves → hypothalamus → posterior pituitary → oxytocin in blood → contraction of smooth muscle of mammary gland → milk let-down. The milkman's cow had milk in the gland but no oxytocin release until the calf provided the stimulus.

ncert_questions.q: A sample of urine was diagnosed to contain high content of glucose and ketone bodies. Based on this observation, answer the following: (a) Which endocrine gland and hormone is related to this condition? (b) Name the cells on which this hormone acts. (c) What is the condition called and how can it be rectified?
ncert_questions.a: (a) The pancreas (its endocrine part, the islets of Langerhans, specifically the β-cells) and the hormone insulin. (b) Insulin acts mainly on hepatocytes (liver cells) and adipocytes (fat cells), increasing their uptake of glucose and stimulating glycogenesis. (c) The condition is diabetes mellitus. Insulin deficiency (or resistance) causes prolonged hyperglycemia; the glucose exceeds the renal threshold and is lost in urine, and cells that cannot use glucose break down fats, forming ketone bodies. It is rectified by insulin therapy (injection of insulin), along with diet control.

ncert_questions.q: Illustrate the differences between the mechanisms of action of a protein hormone and a steroid hormone.
ncert_questions.a:
Protein (peptide) hormone, e.g. insulin, glucagon, FSH: (i) water-soluble, cannot cross the plasma membrane; (ii) binds to a membrane-bound receptor on the target cell surface; (iii) the hormone-receptor complex generates a second messenger inside the cell (cyclic AMP, IP3 or Ca2+); (iv) the second messenger activates enzyme cascades that regulate cellular metabolism; (v) the response is rapid and does not involve new gene expression directly. Flow: hormone → membrane receptor → second messenger → enzyme activation → physiological response (Fig. 19.5a).

Steroid hormone, e.g. cortisol, testosterone, estradiol (and iodothyronines): (i) lipid-soluble, passes through the plasma membrane; (ii) binds to an intracellular (nuclear) receptor; (iii) the hormone-receptor complex enters the nucleus and interacts with the genome; (iv) regulates gene expression or chromosome function, leading to synthesis of new proteins; (v) the cumulative biochemical actions produce physiological and developmental effects, slower but long lasting. Flow: hormone → intracellular receptor → hormone-receptor complex → genome → gene expression → physiological and developmental effects (Fig. 19.5b).

ncert_questions.q: Hypothalamus is a super master endocrine gland. Elaborate.
ncert_questions.a: The pituitary is called the master gland because its trophic hormones (TSH, ACTH, LH, FSH, GH, prolactin) control the thyroid, adrenal cortex, gonads and other tissues. But the pituitary itself is controlled by the hypothalamus, which is why the hypothalamus is called the super master gland. (i) The hypothalamus contains groups of neurosecretory cells (nuclei) that produce releasing hormones, which stimulate the secretion of anterior pituitary hormones (e.g. GnRH → LH and FSH; TRH → TSH; CRH → ACTH; GHRH → GH), and inhibiting hormones, which inhibit them (e.g. somatostatin → inhibits GH; PIH → inhibits prolactin). (ii) These hormones travel down the axons, are released at the nerve endings and reach the anterior pituitary through the hypophysial portal circulation. (iii) The hypothalamus also synthesises oxytocin and vasopressin, which are transported axonally to and stored in the posterior pituitary, and it controls their release through direct neural connections. (iv) Thus every pituitary hormone, and through them every pituitary-dependent gland, is under hypothalamic control; and the hypothalamus in turn links the endocrine system to the nervous system, receiving neural inputs and feedback from circulating hormones. Hence it is the super master gland.

pyq.q: Which of the following hormones is not secreted by the anterior pituitary (pars distalis)?
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: Oxytocin is synthesised in the hypothalamus and released from the posterior pituitary (neurohypophysis). GH, prolactin, TSH, ACTH, LH and FSH are the six hormones of the pars distalis.

pyq.q: Leydig cells of the testis produce a group of hormones called
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: The interstitial (Leydig) cells in the intertubular spaces of the testis secrete androgens, mainly testosterone. Gonadotrophins come from the pituitary, estrogens from the ovarian follicles.

pyq.q: Which of the following is the correct matching of hormone and effect?
options: Atrial natriuretic factor – increases blood pressure
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: PTH is the hypercalcemic hormone. Glucagon raises blood glucose, ANF lowers blood pressure, and insulin stimulates glycogenesis (not glycogenolysis).

pyq.q: The second messenger in the action of a peptide hormone such as glucagon is
options: The hormone-receptor complex on the nucleus
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: Peptide hormones bind membrane receptors and generate second messengers such as cyclic AMP, IP<sub>3</sub> or Ca<sup>2+</sup>. Adenylate cyclase is the enzyme that makes cAMP, not the messenger.

pyq.q: Which one of the following is a steroid hormone that regulates water and electrolyte balance?
pyq.answer: d
pyq.solution: Aldosterone, the mineralocorticoid of the adrenal cortex, is a steroid that promotes Na<sup>+</sup> and water reabsorption and K<sup>+</sup> excretion. Vasopressin also regulates water but is a peptide.

pyq.q: The outermost layer of the adrenal cortex is the
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: From outside inward the cortex has the zona glomerulosa, zona fasciculata and zona reticularis; the medulla is the central tissue, not part of the cortex.

pyq.q: Which of the following conditions is NOT a result of thyroid hormone deficiency?
pyq.answer: d
pyq.solution: Exophthalmic goitre (Graves' disease) is a form of hyperthyroidism, an excess of thyroid hormones. Cretinism, iodine-deficiency goitre and myxoedema are due to hypothyroidism.

pyq.q: Erythropoietin, the hormone that stimulates RBC formation, is secreted by
options: The atrial wall of the heart
The juxtaglomerular cells of the kidney
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: The juxtaglomerular cells of the kidney secrete erythropoietin, which acts on the bone marrow to stimulate erythropoiesis. The atrial wall secretes ANF.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): The posterior pituitary is not a true endocrine gland. Reason (R): Oxytocin and vasopressin are synthesised in the hypothalamus and only stored in and released from the posterior pituitary.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: The neurohypophysis does not synthesise any hormone; the two hormones it releases are made by hypothalamic neurosecretory cells and transported axonally to it. R correctly explains A.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): Adrenaline is called the emergency hormone. Reason (R): Adrenaline is a steroid hormone secreted by the adrenal cortex.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: Adrenaline is indeed the emergency (fight or flight) hormone, but it is an amino-acid derivative (catecholamine) secreted by the adrenal medulla, not a steroid of the cortex. A is true, R is false.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): Steroid hormones act by regulating gene expression in the target cell. Reason (R): Steroid hormones are lipid-soluble, cross the plasma membrane and bind to intracellular receptors.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: Because they enter the cell and form a hormone-receptor complex that interacts with the genome, steroids regulate gene expression. R is the reason for A.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): Diabetes insipidus is treated by insulin injection. Reason (R): Diabetes insipidus is caused by the deficiency of vasopressin (ADH).
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: d
pyq.solution: Diabetes insipidus results from ADH deficiency, so R is true; it has nothing to do with insulin, which treats diabetes mellitus, so A is false.

pyq.q: Why is the pancreas called a composite (heterocrine) gland? Name the two types of cells of its endocrine part and the hormone each secretes.
pyq.answer: The pancreas acts as both an exocrine gland (the acini secrete pancreatic juice into the duodenum through the pancreatic duct) and an endocrine gland (the islets of Langerhans secrete hormones into the blood), so it is a composite or heterocrine gland. In the islets, the α-cells secrete glucagon and the β-cells secrete insulin.

pyq.q: Name the hormone secreted by the pineal gland and state two functions of it.
pyq.answer: The pineal gland secretes melatonin.
