Functions: (i) it regulates the 24-hour (diurnal) rhythm of the body, maintaining the normal rhythms of the sleep-wake cycle and of body temperature; (ii) it also influences metabolism, pigmentation, the menstrual cycle and the body's defence capability.

pyq.q: How do hypothalamic hormones reach the anterior pituitary? How does the hypothalamus control the posterior pituitary?
pyq.answer: Hypothalamic releasing and inhibiting hormones are released from the axon endings of the neurosecretory cells and are carried to the anterior pituitary (pars distalis) through the hypophysial portal circulation, a system of blood vessels connecting the two. The posterior pituitary (neurohypophysis) is under the direct neural regulation of the hypothalamus: the axons of hypothalamic neurons run into it and release oxytocin and vasopressin there.

pyq.q: Distinguish between diabetes mellitus and diabetes insipidus.
pyq.answer: Diabetes mellitus is caused by deficiency of insulin (or insulin resistance); blood glucose stays high, glucose appears in urine and ketone bodies form; treated by insulin therapy. Diabetes insipidus is caused by deficiency of vasopressin (ADH); water reabsorption in the distal tubules falls, so a large volume of dilute urine is passed (diuresis) with intense thirst, but urine contains no glucose and blood sugar is normal.

pyq.q: Name the four hormones of the gastrointestinal tract and give the function of any two.
pyq.answer: Gastrin, secretin, cholecystokinin (CCK) and gastric inhibitory peptide (GIP). Gastrin acts on the gastric glands and stimulates secretion of HCl and pepsinogen. Secretin acts on the exocrine pancreas and stimulates secretion of water and bicarbonate ions. (CCK stimulates pancreatic enzymes and bile release; GIP inhibits gastric secretion and motility.)

pyq.q: Describe the role of parathyroid hormone and calcitonin in maintaining the blood calcium level.
pyq.answer: Blood calcium is held within a narrow range by two antagonistic hormones. (i) When blood Ca2+ falls, the four parathyroid glands secrete parathyroid hormone (PTH), a peptide. PTH raises blood calcium by three routes: it stimulates bone resorption (dissolution, demineralisation) releasing Ca2+ into blood; it increases reabsorption of Ca2+ by the renal tubules; and it increases absorption of Ca2+ from digested food in the intestine. PTH is therefore a hypercalcemic hormone. (ii) When blood Ca2+ rises, the thyroid gland secretes thyrocalcitonin (calcitonin), a protein hormone, which suppresses the release of calcium from bone and lowers blood calcium. (iii) The two act in opposite directions, and the secretion of each is regulated directly by the circulating level of Ca2+, so together they maintain calcium homeostasis needed for muscle contraction, nerve conduction and blood clotting.

pyq.q: Explain how insulin and glucagon together maintain the blood glucose level. What happens when insulin is deficient?
pyq.answer: After a meal blood glucose rises; the β-cells of the islets of Langerhans secrete insulin, a peptide hormone, which acts on hepatocytes and adipocytes, increasing their uptake and utilisation of glucose and stimulating glycogenesis (glucose → glycogen). Blood glucose falls, so insulin is hypoglycemic. Between meals blood glucose falls; the α-cells secrete glucagon, which acts on the liver, stimulating glycogenolysis (glycogen → glucose) and gluconeogenesis (glucose from non-carbohydrate sources) and reducing cellular glucose uptake. Blood glucose rises, so glucagon is hyperglycemic. The two antagonistic hormones thus keep blood glucose steady. When insulin is deficient, prolonged hyperglycemia results, glucose is lost in urine and harmful ketone bodies are formed; this is diabetes mellitus, treated by insulin therapy.

pyq.q: A student is about to appear for an interview and notices sweating, a racing heart and rapid breathing. Name the hormones responsible, the gland that secretes them, and list four other effects they produce.
pyq.answer: The hormones are adrenaline (epinephrine) and noradrenaline (norepinephrine), the catecholamines secreted by the adrenal medulla in response to stress; they are called emergency hormones or hormones of fight or flight. Besides sweating, increased heart beat and increased rate of respiration, they (i) increase alertness, (ii) dilate the pupils, (iii) cause piloerection, (iv) increase the strength of heart contraction, and (v) stimulate glycogenolysis, lipolysis and proteolysis, raising the blood glucose available for a quick response.

pyq.q: State the functions of the two groups of corticoids secreted by the adrenal cortex.
pyq.answer: The adrenal cortex secretes steroid hormones called corticoids. Glucocorticoids (mainly cortisol) are involved in carbohydrate metabolism: they stimulate gluconeogenesis, lipolysis and proteolysis and inhibit cellular uptake and utilisation of amino acids; cortisol also maintains cardiovascular and kidney functions, produces anti-inflammatory reactions, suppresses the immune response and stimulates RBC production. Mineralocorticoids (mainly aldosterone) regulate water and electrolyte balance: aldosterone acts on the renal tubules to stimulate reabsorption of Na+ and water and excretion of K+ and phosphate ions, thereby maintaining electrolytes, body fluid volume, osmotic pressure and blood pressure. The cortex also secretes small amounts of androgens that promote growth of axial, pubic and facial hair at puberty.

pyq.q: Differentiate between hypothyroidism and hyperthyroidism, naming one disorder of each.
pyq.answer: Hypothyroidism is the under-secretion of thyroid hormones (T3, T4), most often from dietary iodine deficiency. Effects: goitre (enlarged thyroid), low BMR, and in a foetus or child cretinism (stunted growth, mental retardation, low IQ, abnormal skin, deaf-mutism); in adults myxoedema and, in women, irregular menstrual cycles. Hyperthyroidism is the over-secretion of thyroid hormones, due to thyroid cancer or nodules of the thyroid. Effects: raised BMR, weight loss, and exophthalmic goitre (Graves' disease) with enlarged thyroid and protruding eyeballs. Hypothyroidism is prevented by iodised salt; hyperthyroidism needs medical treatment of the gland.

pyq.q: Describe the structure of the pituitary gland and the hormones secreted by each of its parts, with their functions. Explain the relationship of the pituitary with the hypothalamus.
pyq.answer:
Structure. The pituitary lies in the sella turcica, a bony cavity, attached to the hypothalamus by a stalk. It has an adenohypophysis, made of the pars distalis (anterior pituitary) and pars intermedia, and a neurohypophysis (pars nervosa, posterior pituitary).

Pars distalis secretes six hormones: growth hormone (body growth; excess gives gigantism in children and acromegaly in adults, deficiency gives pituitary dwarfism); prolactin (growth of mammary glands and milk formation); TSH (synthesis and secretion of thyroid hormones); ACTH (secretion of glucocorticoids from the adrenal cortex); LH and FSH, the gonadotrophins (LH: androgen secretion in males, ovulation and corpus luteum maintenance in females; FSH: spermatogenesis with androgens in males, growth of ovarian follicles in females). Pars intermedia secretes MSH, which acts on melanocytes and regulates skin pigmentation.

Neurohypophysis stores and releases oxytocin (contraction of uterine smooth muscle at child birth and milk ejection) and vasopressin/ADH (reabsorption of water and electrolytes by the distal tubules, reducing diuresis; deficiency causes diabetes insipidus). These two are synthesised in the hypothalamus and transported axonally.

Relationship with the hypothalamus. Neurosecretory cells of the hypothalamus produce releasing hormones (e.g. GnRH) and inhibiting hormones (e.g. somatostatin) which reach the anterior pituitary by the hypophysial portal circulation and control its secretion. The posterior pituitary is controlled by direct neural connections. Hence the pituitary is the master gland and the hypothalamus the super master gland. Draw NCERT Fig. 19.2 showing the neurosecretory cells, the portal vessels to the anterior lobe and the axons to the posterior lobe.

pyq.q: With a labelled diagram describe the structure of the adrenal gland and the hormones secreted by its two parts.
pyq.answer:
Structure. A pair of adrenal glands lies at the anterior (upper) part of each kidney. Each has a central adrenal medulla and an outer adrenal cortex. The cortex has three layers, from outside in: zona glomerulosa, zona fasciculata and zona reticularis. Draw NCERT Fig. 19.4 with the capsule, the three cortical zones and the medulla labelled.

Adrenal medulla secretes adrenaline (epinephrine) and noradrenaline (norepinephrine), the catecholamines, rapidly in response to stress and emergency; hence they are emergency hormones or hormones of fight or flight. They increase alertness, dilate the pupils, cause piloerection and sweating, increase the heart beat and the strength of heart contraction, increase the rate of respiration, and stimulate glycogenolysis (raising blood glucose), lipolysis and proteolysis.

Adrenal cortex secretes steroid hormones, the corticoids. Glucocorticoids (cortisol) regulate carbohydrate metabolism: gluconeogenesis, lipolysis, proteolysis, inhibition of amino-acid uptake; cortisol also maintains cardiovascular and kidney function, is anti-inflammatory, suppresses immunity and stimulates RBC production. Mineralocorticoids (aldosterone) act on the renal tubules to reabsorb Na+ and water and excrete K+ and phosphate, maintaining electrolytes, fluid volume, osmotic pressure and blood pressure. Small amounts of androgenic steroids promote growth of axial, pubic and facial hair at puberty. The cortex is controlled by ACTH of the pituitary; the medulla by sympathetic nerves.

pyq.q: Explain the mechanism of hormone action. Classify hormones on the basis of chemical nature and show, with diagrams, how a protein hormone and a steroid hormone act on their target cells.
pyq.answer:
Hormones act by binding to specific protein receptors present only in target tissues. Receptors are either membrane-bound (on the plasma membrane) or intracellular (mostly in the nucleus, hence nuclear receptors). Each receptor is specific to one hormone. Binding forms a hormone-receptor complex, which triggers biochemical changes in the target tissue and so regulates its metabolism and physiological functions.

Chemical classes: (i) peptide, polypeptide and protein hormones (insulin, glucagon, pituitary and hypothalamic hormones); (ii) steroids (cortisol, testosterone, estradiol, progesterone); (iii) iodothyronines (thyroid hormones); (iv) amino-acid derivatives (epinephrine).

Protein hormone (Fig. 19.5a): being water-soluble it cannot enter the cell. It binds to a membrane-bound receptor; the complex generates a second messenger (cyclic AMP, IP3 or Ca2+) inside the cell; the second messenger activates enzyme cascades that regulate cellular metabolism and produce the physiological response. Draw: hormone outside → receptor in membrane → second messenger → enzyme activation → response.

Steroid hormone (Fig. 19.5b): being lipid-soluble it passes through the plasma membrane and binds to an intracellular receptor; the hormone-receptor complex enters the nucleus and interacts with the genome, regulating gene expression or chromosome function; the cumulative biochemical actions (synthesis of specific proteins) result in physiological and developmental effects. Draw: hormone crossing membrane → receptor in cytoplasm/nucleus → complex on DNA → gene expression → protein → effects. Iodothyronines act like steroids. The protein-hormone pathway is fast and short-lived; the steroid pathway is slower and long lasting.

pyq.q:
Read the passage and answer the questions. A 35-year-old woman from a hilly village complains of tiredness, weight gain, intolerance to cold and a visible swelling in the front of her neck. Blood tests show low thyroxine and a high level of TSH. Her family eats non-iodised rock salt. She is in the third month of pregnancy.
(i) Name the condition and state the cause of the neck swelling.
(ii) Why is TSH high when thyroxine is low?
(iii) Name the hormone of the thyroid that is NOT affected by iodine deficiency and state its function.
(iv) What risk does her condition pose to the baby? Name the disorder and two of its features.
pyq.answer:
(i) Hypothyroidism with goitre; the swelling is the enlarged thyroid gland caused by deficiency of iodine in the diet, which is essential for thyroxine synthesis.
(ii) Thyroxine normally inhibits the release of TRH and TSH by negative feedback. When thyroxine is low the inhibition is lost, so the pituitary secretes more TSH; the excess TSH over-stimulates the thyroid, and the gland enlarges.
(iii) Thyrocalcitonin (calcitonin), a protein hormone that does not contain iodine; it lowers the blood calcium level.
(iv) Hypothyroidism during pregnancy causes defective development and maturation of the foetus, leading to cretinism: stunted growth, mental retardation, low IQ, abnormal skin, deaf-mutism (any two). Iodised salt or thyroxine supplementation prevents it.

pyq.q:
Read the passage and answer the questions. Two hormones from different glands act on the kidney. Hormone P is released when blood pressure rises and causes blood vessels to dilate. Hormone Q is released from the posterior pituitary when the body is dehydrated and makes the distal tubules reabsorb more water. A patient with a head injury damaging the hypothalamus begins to pass 8 to 10 litres of dilute urine a day and is constantly thirsty, though her blood sugar is normal.
(i) Identify hormones P and Q and the gland or tissue that secretes each.
(ii) Name the patient's condition and explain why the urine is dilute and copious.
(iii) Why did damage to the hypothalamus, and not to the posterior pituitary itself, produce this condition?
(iv) Name one other hormone that acts on the renal tubules and state its effect.
pyq.answer:
(i) P is atrial natriuretic factor (ANF), secreted by the atrial wall of the heart. Q is vasopressin or anti-diuretic hormone (ADH), synthesised in the hypothalamus and released from the posterior pituitary (neurohypophysis).
(ii) Diabetes insipidus. Without ADH the distal tubules (and collecting ducts) do not reabsorb water, so most of the filtrate is lost as a large volume of dilute urine (diuresis); the water loss causes thirst. There is no glucose in the urine because insulin is normal.
(iii) ADH is not made by the posterior pituitary; it is synthesised by the neurosecretory cells of the hypothalamus and transported along their axons to be stored in the posterior pituitary. Damage to the hypothalamus stops its synthesis, so the store is not replenished.
(iv) Aldosterone (adrenal cortex) stimulates reabsorption of Na+ and water and excretion of K+ by the renal tubules; or parathyroid hormone increases Ca2+ reabsorption by the renal tubules (either one).

practice_mcq.q: Hormones are best defined as
options: Nutrient chemicals produced in large amounts by ducted glands
Non-nutrient chemicals acting as intercellular messengers and produced in trace amounts
practice_mcq.explanation: This is the NCERT definition; each phrase (non-nutrient, intercellular messenger, trace amounts) is a marking point.

practice_mcq.q: Somatostatin secreted by the hypothalamus
practice_mcq.explanation: NCERT gives somatostatin as the example of an inhibiting hormone: it inhibits the release of GH from the pituitary. GnRH is the example of a releasing hormone.

practice_mcq.q: The pituitary gland is located in a bony cavity called the
practice_mcq.explanation: The pituitary sits in the sella turcica of the sphenoid bone and is attached to the hypothalamus by a stalk.

practice_mcq.q: Excess secretion of growth hormone in a middle-aged adult leads to
practice_mcq.explanation: After the growth plates close, excess GH cannot lengthen bones; it thickens them, especially in the face, producing acromegaly. Gigantism is GH excess in childhood.

practice_mcq.q: Which pair of hormones is synthesised in the hypothalamus but released from the posterior pituitary?
practice_mcq.explanation: The neurohypophysis stores and releases oxytocin and vasopressin, which are transported axonally from the hypothalamic neurosecretory cells.

practice_mcq.q: Melanocyte stimulating hormone is secreted by the
practice_mcq.explanation: MSH comes from the pars intermedia of the adenohypophysis, which in humans is almost merged with the pars distalis. The pineal secretes melatonin, a different molecule.

practice_mcq.q: Thyroid hormones are synthesised by the
practice_mcq.explanation: The follicular cells of the thyroid follicles synthesise T<sub>3</sub> and T<sub>4</sub>; the parafollicular (C) cells make calcitonin; chief cells are in the parathyroid.

practice_mcq.q: Which of the following is a protein hormone that lowers blood calcium?
practice_mcq.explanation: Thyrocalcitonin (calcitonin) from the thyroid is a protein hormone that regulates blood calcium by lowering it; PTH raises it.

practice_mcq.q: The number of parathyroid glands in a human and their position are
options: Two, in front of the thyroid
Four, on the back of the thyroid
practice_mcq.explanation: Four parathyroid glands lie on the back side of the thyroid, one pair in each lobe.

practice_mcq.q: Thymosins are responsible for
practice_mcq.explanation: Thymosins from the thymus bring about differentiation of T-lymphocytes for cell-mediated immunity and also promote antibody production.

practice_mcq.q: Adrenaline and noradrenaline are chemically
practice_mcq.explanation: The catecholamines are derived from the amino acid tyrosine; NCERT places epinephrine in the amino-acid-derivative class.

practice_mcq.q: Cortisol is secreted mainly by the
practice_mcq.explanation: The middle zona fasciculata secretes glucocorticoids such as cortisol; the outer glomerulosa secretes aldosterone and the inner reticularis small amounts of androgens.

practice_mcq.q: Which hormone reduces the cellular uptake and utilisation of glucose?
practice_mcq.explanation: Glucagon, besides stimulating glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis, reduces cellular glucose uptake; insulin does the opposite.

practice_mcq.q: The islets of Langerhans constitute about what fraction of the pancreatic tissue?
practice_mcq.explanation: About 1 to 2 million islets are present, yet they represent only 1 to 2 per cent of the pancreatic tissue.

practice_mcq.q: In females, luteinising hormone
options: Stimulates growth of the ovarian follicles only
Induces ovulation and maintains the corpus luteum
practice_mcq.explanation: LH induces ovulation of the fully mature Graafian follicle and maintains the corpus luteum; FSH stimulates follicle growth; prolactin stimulates milk formation.

practice_mcq.q: Estrogen is secreted mainly by the
practice_mcq.explanation: Growing ovarian follicles secrete estrogen; after ovulation the corpus luteum secretes mainly progesterone.

practice_mcq.q: Which hormone stimulates the secretion of pancreatic enzymes and bile juice?
practice_mcq.explanation: CCK acts on both the pancreas and the gall bladder. Secretin stimulates water and bicarbonate from the pancreas; gastrin stimulates HCl and pepsinogen.

practice_mcq.q: Which of the following hormones binds to an intracellular receptor?
practice_mcq.explanation: Iodothyronines and steroids are lipid-soluble and use intracellular (nuclear) receptors to regulate gene expression; insulin, glucagon and adrenaline use membrane receptors and second messengers.

practice_mcq.q: Which of these organs does NOT show a cortex and medulla arrangement?
practice_mcq.explanation: The adrenal, kidney and ovary each have an outer cortex and an inner medulla; the liver is organised into lobules with no cortex-medulla division.

practice_mcq.q: Atrial natriuretic factor is secreted when
practice_mcq.explanation: ANF from the atrial wall is released when blood pressure increases; it dilates blood vessels and brings the pressure down.

common_mistakes: Writing that the posterior pituitary secretes or produces oxytocin and vasopressin. It only stores and releases them; they are synthesised in the hypothalamus. The examiner deducts for 'secreted by the posterior pituitary' in a 2-mark answer.
Mixing up melanin, melatonin and MSH. Melatonin is the pineal hormone for the sleep-wake rhythm; MSH is the pituitary hormone acting on melanocytes; melanin is the pigment, not a hormone.
Attaching the three 'glyco' words to the wrong hormone. Glucagon does glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis; insulin does glycogenesis. Reversing them turns a correct mechanism into a wrong one.

Naming the adrenal cortex layers in the wrong order or calling the zona reticularis the outer layer. From outside in it is glomerulosa, fasciculata, reticularis; NCERT lists them from the inside, which is where the confusion starts.
Confusing diabetes mellitus (insulin, glucose in urine, ketone bodies) with diabetes insipidus (ADH, large volumes of dilute urine, no sugar). Case questions are built on this contrast.

Saying that hypothalamic hormones reach the anterior pituitary 'through the blood' without the word portal, or saying the posterior pituitary is also reached by the portal system. Anterior = portal circulation; posterior = neural (axonal) connection.

Giving only one route for PTH. Full marks need all three: bone resorption, renal tubular reabsorption and intestinal absorption of Ca<sup>2+</sup>. Also, PTH raises calcium and calcitonin lowers it; students reverse them under pressure.

Placing steroid hormone receptors on the membrane or making protein hormones act on the genome. Protein hormones stay outside the cell and use second messengers; steroids and iodothyronines enter and regulate gene expression. In the diagram, drawing insulin inside the cell loses the mark.
Writing 'exophthalmic goitre' as a hypothyroid condition. It is Graves' disease, a form of hyperthyroidism; only cretinism, myxoedema and simple goitre are due to deficiency.
Assigning erythropoietin to the bone marrow or to the heart. It comes from the juxtaglomerular cells of the kidney and acts on the marrow; ANF is the heart's hormone.
strategy:
This chapter is a memory chapter with one conceptual section at the end, so plan it that way. Spend the first sitting building a single table with seven columns: gland, location, hormone, chemical class, target, effect, disorder. Fill it from NCERT in NCERT order, hypothalamus to ovary and then heart, kidney and gut. Everything objective in the paper, every MCQ, every Assertion-Reason, every fill-in-the-blank, is a cell of that table, and writing it out yourself once beats reading it five times.

Second sitting: the two diagrams that carry 5-mark questions. Draw the hypothalamus-pituitary figure until you can produce the two routes (portal vessels to the anterior lobe, axons to the posterior lobe) without looking, and draw the adrenal section with its three zonae and the hormones of each written beside them. Then draw the pair of mechanism diagrams, protein hormone and steroid hormone, side by side. These three drawings plus the location figure cover every diagram the school paper has ever asked from this chapter.

Third sitting: the antagonistic pairs and the disorders. Insulin versus glucagon, PTH versus calcitonin, ANF versus aldosterone and ADH. For each disorder learn the hormone, the direction (excess or deficiency) and two symptoms: gigantism, dwarfism, acromegaly, diabetes insipidus, goitre, cretinism, myxoedema, Graves' disease, diabetes mellitus. Then work through the nine NCERT exercise questions and the exemplar long answers given above, especially the milking reflex, the glucose-and-ketone urine sample and the super master gland, because schools lift them almost unchanged.

In the exam, give 1-mark items ten seconds each; the answer is either in your table or it is not. Write 3-mark answers as three numbered points with the NCERT verb in each (stimulates, inhibits, reabsorbs). For a 5-mark diagram question, draw first, label in pencil-neat capitals, and only then write the text; a clean labelled figure earns two of the five marks on its own.
revision_checklist: NCERT definition of a hormone (non-nutrient, intercellular messenger, trace amounts) and the exocrine versus endocrine contrast
Location of all endocrine glands on the body outline: pineal, hypothalamus, pituitary, thyroid, parathyroid, thymus, adrenal, pancreas, testis or ovary
Hypothalamus: neurosecretory cells; GnRH (releasing) and somatostatin (inhibiting); portal circulation to the anterior lobe; axons to the posterior lobe
Pituitary parts: pars distalis (GH, PRL, TSH, ACTH, LH, FSH), pars intermedia (MSH), neurohypophysis (oxytocin, vasopressin made in the hypothalamus)
GH disorders: gigantism, pituitary dwarfism, acromegaly; ADH deficiency gives diabetes insipidus
Pineal: melatonin, 24-hour rhythm, sleep-wake cycle and body temperature; jet lag explanation
Thyroid: lobes and isthmus, follicular cells make T3 and T4, iodine essential; calcitonin lowers calcium; functions (BMR, RBC formation, metabolism, water-electrolyte balance)
Thyroid disorders: goitre, cretinism (five features), myxoedema, hyperthyroidism, exophthalmic goitre = Graves' disease
Parathyroid: four glands, PTH raises Ca2+ by bone resorption, renal reabsorption, intestinal absorption; antagonist of calcitonin
Thymus: dorsal to heart and aorta, thymosins, T-cell differentiation and antibody production, degenerates with age
Adrenal medulla: adrenaline and noradrenaline, all fight-or-flight effects, glycogenolysis, lipolysis, proteolysis
Adrenal cortex: glomerulosa, fasciculata, reticularis; cortisol functions; aldosterone functions; small androgens
Pancreas: composite gland, islets 1 to 2 per cent, alpha glucagon (hyperglycemic), beta insulin (hypoglycemic), diabetes mellitus with ketone bodies
Testis: Leydig cells, testosterone functions; ovary: follicles estrogen, corpus luteum progesterone; roles of LH and FSH in each sex
Non-endocrine sources: ANF (atrium), erythropoietin (kidney JG cells), gastrin, secretin, CCK, GIP; growth factors
Four chemical classes of hormones with one example each; membrane receptor plus second messenger (cAMP, IP3, Ca2+) versus intracellular receptor plus gene expression
The four labelled diagrams: gland locations, hypothalamus-pituitary, adrenal section, protein versus steroid hormone action
